name: Brow henna

lead: Brow henna is a paste made from powdered henna leaves that stains brow hairs and the skin underneath, making brows look darker and more filled in. It is done in salons or with at-home kits.
The colour is temporary, with the skin stain generally fading over one to three weeks. No clinical studies specific to eyebrow henna were found.

paras: The lawsone dye in henna binds to the keratin in hair and the outer skin layer, producing an orange-to-reddish-brown stain that darkens over a few days.

Natural henna is regarded differently from products sold as black henna, which often contain PPD and have been linked to severe allergic reactions and scarring. The US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application.

lead: Brow henna, also called henna brows, is a semi-permanent way of tinting eyebrow hair and the skin beneath it using a paste made from the powdered leaves of the henna plant. It is offered mainly by brow salons and is also sold as an at-home kit, and it is used to make sparse or light brows look darker and fuller.[1]

Henna has a long history as a dye for hair, skin and nails, originating in North Africa and the Middle East.[1] Wikipedia notes that its use as a temporary substitute for eyebrow pencil is comparatively recent.[1] The stain sits on the outer layer of skin and fades over roughly one to three weeks, with the skin stain usually fading sooner than the colour on hair.[1]

No clinical studies of henna specifically for eyebrows were found. Regulators distinguish natural henna from so-called black henna, which often contains para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and has been linked to severe allergic reactions; the US FDA has not approved henna for direct application to skin.[1]

paras: Brow henna uses a paste of dried, powdered henna leaf applied to the brow hairs and underlying skin. The pigment stains the outer skin layer and the hair, filling gaps in the brow shape and darkening pale or fine hairs. On skin, henna stain typically starts orange and darkens to reddish brown over about three days before fading over one to three weeks.[1]

Henna on hair gives results ranging from orange to burgundy depending on the starting colour, and practitioners sometimes blend it with other plant dyes such as cassia or indigo to change the shade.[1]

Ancient Egyptians used henna on hair, skin and nails, and its use later spread through the Maghreb, the Indian subcontinent and parts of Eastern Europe.[1] Eyebrow darkening itself has older roots in cosmetics such as kohl, and brow styling has varied between eras, from the 1920s-30s fashion for thin plucked brows to the Elizabethan practice of removing brows entirely.[2] Henna as a modern brow product is described as a recent development.[1]

Some products sold as henna contain metal salts, oils or waxes, or allergenic dyes. Products marketed as black henna often contain little or no henna and may include PPD at concentrations of 10 percent to 80 percent, compared with a limit below 6 percent for hair dyes.[1] Reactions to PPD commonly appear 3 to 12 days after application and can include blistering and permanent scarring, and sensitisation can be lifelong, affecting later exposure to hair dyes.[1]

In the United States the FDA allows henna only as a hair dye, has not approved it for direct application to skin, and specifically prohibits PPD as a skin stain.[1] Because brow henna is applied to skin near the eye, product labelling and regulatory status differ by country.
